tagline.text: The Philippines' toughest peak, with knife-edge ridges on Sibuyan Island

location.label: Location
location.text: Central Sibuyan Island, spanning Magdiwang, San Fernando and Cajidiocan

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: February–May dry season (check closure notices for November–January)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱12,000–16,000 (per person, local climbing costs only, excluding travel to the island)

children.text: Mount Guiting-Guiting rises about 2,058 m above sea level on Sibuyan Island in Romblon, and ranks among the Philippines' most demanding climbs. It is a natural park of sharp ridges, rock sections and rare mountain plants, and a permit and a guide are required.

Mount Guiting-Guiting, usually called G2, rises in the middle of Sibuyan Island in Romblon province. At about 2,058 m above sea level, it is the highest point in Romblon. The name is said to mean "jagged" in the Romblon language, and the ridges are indeed like saw teeth. In the Philippine mountaineering community it is rated 9 on a 1–9 difficulty scale, which makes it one of the most challenging climbs in the country. It was designated the Mt. Guiting-Guiting Natural Park in 1996, and the park also includes Mount Nailog (about 789 m) to the west.

There are two main ways up. The Tampayan Trail from Magdiwang in the north is the traditional route and passes Mayo's Peak, the Knife Edge and the 90-degree wall. The Olango Trail from San Fernando in the south climbs through three camps to the summit. Many climbers link the two, going up one and down the other. On either route, expect sharp ultramafic rock, mud and rainy weather. Reaching the summit takes roughly 10–13 hours of hiking, and the climb is usually done over three days.

Beyond the trails themselves, the park's natural value sets it apart. According to Wikipedia, it holds about 700 species of vascular plants, 54 of them endemic to the island. The pitcher plant Nepenthes sibuyanensis, which grows only on the slopes of the mountain, and Begonia gitingensis are the best-known examples. 130 bird species have been recorded, 102 of which are known or presumed to breed there, and there is also a variety of bats and lizards. The mountain is part of why Sibuyan is nicknamed the "Galapagos of Asia."

What matters most is when and whether you can climb. Wikipedia reports that the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) closes the mountain every year from November to January starting in 2026, for maintenance and rehabilitation. November, when this was written, falls in the closed period, so check the latest notice from the DENR protected area office first when planning. A 2026 guide says that to get a permit you need paperwork such as a medical certificate and proof of earlier difficult climbs, and that climbing alone is prohibited. Requirements change from year to year, so confirm them before you go. The fees and rules in this guide are as checked in 2026.

The highest point in Romblon, the summit sits on a sharp rock ridge. From the top you can take in the shape of the mountains across Sibuyan Island. The summit push is usually started at an early hour.
A narrow ridge between Mayo's Peak and the summit, with drops on both sides. It is described as windy, with no room to use trekking poles. Follow your guide's instructions here and wear a helmet.

blocks.title: The 90-degree wall and Kiss the Wall

children.text: Just below the summit there is a nearly vertical rock wall and a section where you press your body against the rock as you pass. These sections are why the mountain earns its reputation. Some reports say no fixed ropes are installed, so prepare step by step if you have no climbing experience.

. There is a camp near the peak with a good view.

The natural park has about 700 plant species and 130 bird species on record. The endemic Nepenthes sibuyanensis is said to be seen on the slopes near the summit. Do not touch the plants; leave them for photographs.
The Tampayan Trail starts on a long, hot forest path at low elevation and passes through muddy sections with leeches. There are stream crossings and a few water sources.
This trail from San Fernando in the south has camps at
and
. It passes Remvaldely Peak and España Peak on the way to the summit, and is also used as the descent route on a traverse.

Combining the cliff jumps at the Cantingas River, Cresta de Gallo island and Lambingan Falls before or after the climb makes for a fuller island trip. Leave slack in your schedule and stay a day or two longer.

items.subtitle: Up and down the traditional route

children.text: Register at the DENR office in Magdiwang, attend the guide orientation and process your permit. A 2026 guide says climbing on the same day you arrive at the port is prohibited, so arrive a day earlier.
Start from the village of Tampayan and climb the forest trail to camp (near
). Bring gloves and leech socks for the muddy, leech-prone sections.
Set out early and pass Mayo's Peak, the Knife Edge and the 90-degree wall toward the summit. Agree on a turnaround time with your guide for both the way up and the way back.
Descend from the summit, refill water at a spring, and return to camp to rest.
Descend from camp to Tampayan and report your descent at the DENR office. Take a tricycle back to the port.
Times vary greatly with weather and fitness. Follow your guide and DENR instructions for the exact schedule.
Start at Tampayan and climb to Camp 3. Carry water and three days of food.
After the summit push, descend toward the Olango camps, passing ridge and rock sections.
Descend to the village of Olango and move on to San Fernando. The two trailheads are on opposite sides of the island, so arrange return transport in advance.
Take a bus from PITX or elsewhere in Manila to Batangas Port. Fares are reported at about ₱150–270.
From Batangas, Starlite Ferries run to Ambulong Port (Magdiwang) on Sibuyan Island. A 2023 guide gave a
departure (Monday–Saturday), about
9–10 hours
and about ₱1,250, while a 2026 guide gave about
12 hours
and ₱700–1,000, so check the latest schedule.
There is also a route to and from Sibuyan Island on a Starhorse ferry from Lucena (Dalahican). It is reported to take about
16 hours
Check operator notices for sailing days and times. From the port to Tampayan (the northern trailhead) is about
30 minutes
by tricycle or motorbike.
Sibuyan has no scheduled airport. The nearest airport with air service is Tugdan Airport (TBH) on Tablas Island, and you continue to Sibuyan by boat from Romblon or San Agustin.

Boats run to Sibuyan Island from Romblon Island and from Roxas (Panay). A 2023 guide lists Ambulong–Romblon at about ₱250 on Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday and Sunday evenings, and Roxas–Sibuyan at about ₱800.
Magdiwang in the north and San Fernando in the south are linked by jeepney and tricycle, and on rough roads the trip can take 1–2 hours.
To the Olango trailhead in San Fernando you rent a motorbike or tricycle. A 2023 guide gives roughly ₱400–550 per person.

The mountain was long described as open all year, but a notice says that from 2026 climbing is restricted from November to January. The most recent guides name February to May as the safest dry season. One blog recommends December to March, but November to January may be closed, so check.
From June, typhoons and rain raise the risk. If the weather is bad, the guide and the DENR may change or cancel the schedule.

Lodging is in Magdiwang, where you register and meet your guide, and in San Fernando. A travel blog describes a guesthouse in Magdiwang and says Seabreeze Inn in San Fernando charges about ₱800 a night for an air-conditioned double. Names and rates change every year, so check recent reviews on a booking site. A night's stay before the climb is required under the rules.

For the mountain, guides advise bringing three days of food plus one extra day. Small restaurants and shops on Sibuyan sell rice, canned food, snacks and fuel gas. Mobile signal is poor on the ridge, so download your maps in advance.
Check with the DENR protected area office in advance whether climbing is open and what paperwork you need, and prepare it.
One guide says you cannot climb on the day you arrive at the port, so arrive a day early and leave a day of slack.
Bring ankle-supporting hiking boots, a helmet, two pairs of thick gloves and a waterproof jacket. There is rockfall and wind on the Knife Edge.
One guide says the last reliable water is Bulod's Spring near Mayo's Peak. There is no water on the summit section, so carry at least 2 L.
Bring salt or leech socks against leeches.
Agree on a turnaround time with your guide before leaving Mayo's Peak, and keep to it.
Take all your trash with you. Rangers check.
Combine the climb with a dip in the Cantingas River in San Fernando afterward.
G2 is a difficulty-9 climb. The Knife Edge and the 90-degree wall carry a high risk of falling, and some reports say there are no ropes, so do not attempt it without experience.
A DENR permit and a local guide are required, and one guide says climbing alone is prohibited.
A closure from November to January is reported to apply starting in 2026, so plan your dates around the latest notice.
Some sources say only a 3-day itinerary is allowed, and that day hikes and overnight trips are not. Rules may change.
The summit section has no water or mobile signal. Bring a personal first-aid kit and warm gear.
There are reports of local opposition to mining on the island, so follow local news and respect the guidance of villagers.
The fees and rules written here differ between sources and change often. Confirm with the DENR before booking.
